question: Should Arjuna fight the battle in which his elders, teachers and kinsmen stand on the other side?

sides.position: He should not fight: killing his own people brings no good and only sin; he would rather live on alms, or be killed unresisting.
arguments: He sees adverse omens and no good in killing his own people; he wants neither victory, kingship nor pleasures, and would not kill them even for rule over the three worlds (1.31–35).
Sin would come upon them even for killing these aggressors (ātatāyin), and no happiness could follow; seeing the fault, they should turn back (1.36–39, 1.45).

Destroying a family destroys its eternal family dharmas; adharma then prevails, the women are corrupted, the varṇas are mixed, the ancestors fall deprived of their offerings of rice-balls and water, and those whose family dharmas are uprooted dwell in hell — 'so we have heard' (1.40–44).
It would be better to be killed unarmed and unresisting (1.46), or to live on alms than to kill venerable gurus like Bhīṣma and Droṇa and enjoy blood-smeared pleasures (2.4–5).
It is not known which outcome is better, and they would not wish to live after killing them (2.6); no kingdom, even lordship over the gods, would dispel his grief (2.8); 'I will not fight' (2.9).

sides.party: Kṛṣṇa (the teaching of the text; BhG 2.2–3.35)
sides.position: He should stand up and fight, without grief, as his own dharma, with equanimity and without attachment to the fruit, finally resigning all actions to Kṛṣṇa.
arguments: His faintness and unmanliness are unworthy of the noble, do not lead to heaven and bring disgrace (2.2–3).
The wise do not grieve: the embodied one is eternal and neither slays nor is slain; only its bodies have an end, therefore fight (2.11–25, 2.30; esp. 2.18).
Even if the self were born and died again and again, death is certain for the born, so grief would still be unfit (2.26–28).
For a kṣatriya nothing is better than a battle in accordance with dharma; refusing it brings sin and a disgrace worse than death, fighting brings heaven or the earth (2.31–37).
Fighting with pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat made the same incurs no sin (2.38); action done with the right only to the act, not to its fruit, does not bind (2.47–51).
No one can remain without action; allotted action is better than inaction (3.5, 3.8); one should act for the holding together of the world, as Janaka did and as Kṛṣṇa himself does (3.20–24).
Resigning all actions in Kṛṣṇa, free of expectation and of 'mine', fight (3.30); one's own dharma, even deficient, is better than another's well performed (3.35).

notes: A text-internal debate, recorded as the Gītā presents it in chapters 1–3 only; no reconciliation is attempted at extraction. Arjuna's acceptance comes only at the end of the Gītā (18.73, outside this chunk). In ch. 1–3 Kṛṣṇa does not answer the family-dharma argument point by point; at 3.24 he says that if he did not act he would be the maker of saṅkara. The broader epic debate (killing in battle as svadharma vs non-violence as the highest dharma) is dsp:violence-and-svadharma. Merged from A (dsp:should-arjuna-fight) and B (same id as here).

question: Are the Vedic rites that hold out heaven, enjoyment and power all there is to seek ('there is nothing else')?

sides.party: Those who delight in the words of the Veda (vedavādaratāḥ), as the Gītā reports them (BhG 2.42–43)
sides.position: There is nothing else (nānyad astīti): the goal is heaven, enjoyment and power, obtained through the many particular rites, with birth as the fruit of action.
arguments: (Known only through the Gītā's report.) They are full of desire and intent on heaven, hold that there is nothing beyond, and their speech, abounding in particular rites aimed at enjoyment and power, offers birth as the fruit of action (2.42–43).
sides.note: The text names no school; the commentators identify them with those devoted to the ritual portion of the Veda, for whom ritual and its heavenly results are the final aim.

sides.position: Such speech is 'flowery' and proclaimed by the undiscerning; those carried away by it lack resolute understanding established in samādhi; the Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain and one should be free of them; for the knowing brāhmaṇa all the Vedas are of as much use as a well in a flood.
arguments: For those attached to enjoyment and power, whose minds are carried away by that speech, the resolute understanding is not established in samādhi (2.44).
The Vedas have the three guṇas as their domain; be free of the three guṇas and of the pairs of opposites, free of acquiring and keeping, possessed of the self (2.45).
For the knowing brāhmaṇa all the Vedas are of as much use as a well amid a flood (2.46) — a simile the commentators read in opposite directions.
The understanding must become indifferent to what is to be heard and what has been heard, and stand immovable in samādhi though perplexed by what it has heard (2.52–53).

The same speaker enjoins action for the sake of sacrifice and the keeping of the sacrificial wheel (3.9–16); the criticism of 2.42–44 is aimed at those who are desire-souled, intent on heaven and say 'there is nothing else'.

notes: The vedavādins' own texts are not part of this chunk; their side is recorded only as the Gītā reports it (reported_by_opponent). The commentators divide on how sharply 2.45–46 limit the Veda (see the notes on those teachings). Recorded from chapters 1–3 only; no reconciliation is attempted at extraction. Merged from A (dsp:vedic-rites-as-final-goal-bhagavad-gita) and B (same id as here).

question: Is the renunciation of action or the yoga of action better? (BhG 3.1–8, 5.1–6, 6.1–4, 18.1–12)

sides.party: Arjuna's question (BhG 3.1–2), and the view, stated in order to be denied, that renunciation alone brings perfection (3.4)
sides.position: If understanding (buddhi) is held superior to action (cf. 2.49), there is no reason to engage in terrible action; Kṛṣṇa's words seem mixed, and Arjuna asks for the one thing by which he may reach the good.
arguments: Kṛṣṇa himself ranked action far below the yoga of understanding (2.49), yet urges Arjuna to fight (3.1).
The teaching seems mixed and confuses the understanding (3.2).
The view that freedom from action (naiṣkarmya) is reached by not undertaking actions, and perfection by renunciation alone, is mentioned in order to be denied (3.4).

sides.position: There is a twofold commitment, jñāna-yoga for the sāṃkhyas and karma-yoga for the yogins; freedom from action is not reached by not acting, nor perfection by renunciation alone; one must act, for sacrifice and for holding the world together, without attachment.
arguments: A twofold commitment (niṣṭhā) was declared by Kṛṣṇa of old (3.3).
No one attains naiṣkarmya by not undertaking actions, nor perfection by mere renunciation (3.4).
No one can remain even a moment without acting; the guṇas born of prakṛti make all act (3.5).

Outward restraint while the mind dwells on objects is hypocrisy (3.6); action with the organs of action, the senses controlled and without attachment, excels (3.7); action is better than inaction and even bodily life needs it (3.8).
Action for sacrifice done unattached does not bind (3.9).
For one who delights in the self there is nothing to be done (3.17–18); yet act unattached, for by unattached action one attains the highest (3.19).
Janaka and others reached perfection by action; act for lokasaṃgraha, as Kṛṣṇa himself does, without unsettling the understanding of the ignorant (3.20–26).

notes: Contribution of Bhagavad Gītā chapters 1–3 to the skeleton dispute of this id (the question recurs at 5.1–6, 6.1–4 and 18.1–12, outside this chunk). How the two niṣṭhās relate (alternatives for different persons, or stages for one person; whether knowledge alone liberates) is one of the main points on which the Gītā's commentators divide; it bears on the general debate dsp:works-knowledge-grace. No reconciliation is attempted at extraction. Merged from A (dsp:knowledge-or-action-bhagavad-gita) and B (dsp:bhagavad-gita-action-or-renunciation).
